claims.text: The starting material is additively manufactured Al0.2Co1.5CrFeNi1.5Ti0.3 alloy.
The starting alloy retains an fcc matrix.
The starting alloy has a characteristic columnar grain structure resulting from additive manufacturing.
The as-built alloy has high strength.
The as-built alloy has high fatigue performance.
Degradation during elevated-temperature exposure is primarily governed by selective-oxidation-driven elemental segregation.
Under oxidizing conditions, chromium and titanium diffuse toward the alloy surface.
Surface enrichment of chromium and titanium produces a Cr/Ti-rich mixed oxide scale.
The Cr/Ti-rich oxide scale is initially protective.
The oxide scale becomes unstable and spalls during prolonged oxidizing exposure.
Thermal stresses and chemical instability cause oxide-scale spallation.
Selective oxidation locally depletes chromium and titanium in the near-surface region.
Near-surface chromium and titanium depletion alters the local chemistry of the underlying fcc matrix.
Oxide-scale spallation and associated elemental depletion cause degradation of mechanical performance.
After exposure in air at about 900°C for 100 hours, the alloy will exhibit a Cr/Ti-rich oxide layer, scale spallation, and surface microcracking.
Air exposure at about 900°C for 100 hours will reduce fatigue performance and strength relative to the as-built baseline.
Exposure to 5% H2 in N2 suppresses selective oxidation and significant oxide-scale formation relative to air exposure.
Exposure to 5% H2 in N2 better preserves elemental distribution, microstructure, and mechanical integrity than exposure to air.
The proposed mechanism applies around 900°C and approximately 100 hours when comparing high-oxygen-partial-pressure and mildly reducing atmospheres.
Substantially lower temperatures or much shorter exposure times may not produce the same degradation mechanism.
